'''Jeffrey Burke Satinover''' (born September 4, 1947) is an American [[psychiatrist]], [[psychoanalyst]], and [[physicist]]. He is known for books on a number of controversial topics in physics and neuroscience, and on religion, but especially for his writing and public-policy efforts relating to [[homosexuality]], [[same-sex marriage]] and the [[ex-gay movement]].

==Biography==
Satinover was born in Chicago, Illinois, on September 4, 1947, to Joseph and Sena Satinover. He lived in and around Chicago until moving to California at the beginning of his high school years. Satinover won a National Merit Scholarship. He earned his Bachelor of Science degree at the [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]] in 1971. He obtained a [[Ed.M.|Master of Education degree]] in Clinical Psychology and Public Practice from [[Harvard University]], a medical degree at the [[University of Texas]], and a [[Master of Science]] in physics at [[Yale University]]. He received a diploma in analytical psychology from the C. G. Jung Institute of Zürich, becoming their youngest graduate. He trained there and became an accredited Jungian analyst.<ref name=leff>''New York Times'': [https://www.nytimes.com/1982/06/11/style/psychotherapist-weds-julie-leff.html "Psychotherapist Weds Julie Leff," June 11, 1982] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160813192322/http://www.nytimes.com/1982/06/11/style/psychotherapist-weds-julie-leff.html |date=August 13, 2016 }}, accessed March 15, 2012</ref> He received a PhD in physics in the laboratory of [[Didier Sornette]] at the University of Nice in France, in 2009.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.er.ethz.ch/publications/thesis |archive-url=https://archive.today/20130616003249/http://www.er.ethz.ch/publications/thesis |url-status=dead |archive-date=June 16, 2013 |title=ETH – Entrepreneurial Risks – Publications |publisher=Er.ethz.ch |date= |access-date=2013-10-24 }}</ref>

He married for the second time in 1982, having previously divorced and is the father of three daughters.<ref name=leff />
According to two journalists,<ref>Jane Mayer and Jill Abramson, ''Strange Justice: The Selling of Clarence Thomas'' (Boston: Houghton Mifflin, 1994), 306–09.</ref> in September 1991, during the confirmation hearings for U.S. Supreme Court Justice [[Clarence Thomas]], Satinover suggested during dinner conversation with President Bush's nephew<ref>Timothy M. Phelps and Helen Winternitz, ''Capitol Games'', Hyperion (1992) p. 361</ref> that [[Anita Hill]], if suffering from [[erotomania]] (a "[[delusional disorder]]"), might be entirely convinced that Thomas had sexually harassed her, even if he had not, just as a witness for Thomas, [[John Doggett (columnist)|John Doggett]] (now a conservative commentator), claimed had happened with him. She would even pass a lie detector test, as Hill had, convinced of the truth of what she was saying. Soon Satinover and another psychiatrist, [[Park Dietz]] were explaining this possibility to Thomas' Senate sponsor, [[John Danforth]], and White House press secretary, Larry Thomas,<ref>Andrew Peyton Thomas, ''Clarence Thomas: a biography''. Encounter Books (2001) pp. 442–448</ref> though as psychiatrists neither would testify about a patient they had not examined. (Psychiatrists brought in by the Democrats similarly refused to testify.<ref>Herb Kutchin and Stuart Kirk, ''Making Us Crazy'', Simon and Schuster (2003), pp. 1–6</ref>) Satinover was quoted as stating that once he saw the testimony of one of Hill's main critics, [[John Doggett (columnist)|John Doggett]], he concluded the idea was invalid.<ref>{{cite news|title=The Thomas Nomination; Parade of Witnesses Support Hill's Story, Thomas' Integrity|author=Adam Clymer|newspaper=[[The New York Times]]|date=October 14, 1991|access-date=March 28, 2012|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1991/10/14/us/thomas-nomination-parade-witnesses-support-hill-s-story-thomas-s-integrity.html|archive-date=March 25, 2014|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140325215754/http://www.nytimes.com/1991/10/14/us/thomas-nomination-parade-witnesses-support-hill-s-story-thomas-s-integrity.html|url-status=live}}</ref>

He has provided commentary for two documentary films, ''[[What the Bleep Do We Know?!|What the #$*! Do We (K)now!?]]'' (2004) and ''What the Bleep!?: Down the Rabbit Hole '' (2006).<ref>Internet Movie Database: [https://www.imdb.com/name/nm1688748/ Jeffrey Satinover ] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170217113624/http://www.imdb.com/name/nm1688748/ |date=2017-02-17 }}, accessed March 15, 2012</ref>

In 2008, he completed a Ph.D. ''summa cum laude'' in physics at the [[University of Nice]], France.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.tkc.edu/media/archives2.asp?id=123 |title=TKC: Provost Marvin Olasky announces faculty appointments |publisher=Tkc.edu |date= |access-date=2013-12-30 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131230233404/http://www.tkc.edu/media/archives2.asp?id=123 |archive-date=2013-12-30 }}</ref>

Satinover was distinguished visiting professor of Math and Science at [[The King's College (New York)|King's College]], New York City, a private Christian college affiliated with [[Campus Crusade for Christ]]. He also teaches at the [[C. G. Jung Institute in Zürich]]. He is a visiting scientist at the Department of Management, Technology and Economics of the [[ETH Zurich|Swiss Federal Institute of Technology]].<ref>Social Science Research Network: [https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/cf_dev/AbsByAuth.cfm?per_id=1430859 Jeffrey Satinover] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230531092118/https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/cf_dev/AbsByAuth.cfm?per_id=1430859 |date=2023-05-31 }}, accessed March 27, 2012</ref> He is managing director of Quintium Analytics, LLC, a proprietary investment advisory company he founded in 2007. Satinover was a member of the scientific advisory committee of the [[National Association for Research & Therapy of Homosexuality]].<ref>{{cite web |url=http://narth.com/menus/advisors.html |title=NARTH Scientific Advisory Committee |publisher=Narth.com |date= |access-date=2013-12-30 |archive-date=2013-12-03 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131203011346/http://www.narth.com/menus/advisors.html |url-status=live }}</ref>

Satinover is Jewish, but says he has an eclectic worldview.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.virtueonline.org/jewish-psychiatrist-influenced-cs-lewis-says-gays-can-change|title=Jewish Psychiatrist, Influenced by CS Lewis, says gays can change|last=Virtue|first=David|date=2009|website=|publisher=|access-date=June 2, 2016}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=http://thinkprogress.org/lgbt/2013/02/28/1653911/ex-gay-advocates-claim-homosexuality-is-caused-by-parental-abuse/ |title=Ex-Gay Advocates Claim Homosexuality Is Caused By Parental Abuse {{!}} ThinkProgress |website=thinkprogress.org |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130302034507/http://thinkprogress.org/lgbt/2013/02/28/1653911/ex-gay-advocates-claim-homosexuality-is-caused-by-parental-abuse/ |archive-date=2013-03-02}} </ref>

==Writing and research==
Satinover's book, ''Homosexuality and the Politics of Truth'' (1996), published by the [[evangelical Christian]] publisher [[Baker Books]], debates the nature of homosexuality from psychological, religious and scientific perspectives, discussing homosexuality primarily in the context of being a condition that can or should be treated, contrary to the views of the mainstream psychiatric and psychological community.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.apa.org/helpcenter/sexual-orientation.aspx |title=Sexual orientation, homosexuality and bisexuality |publisher=[[American Psychological Association]] |date= |access-date=2012-08-04 |archive-date=2013-08-08 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130808032050/http://www.apa.org/helpcenter/sexual-orientation.aspx |url-status=live }}</ref> Satinover draws comparisons between homosexuality and various pathologies (''e.g.,'' alcoholism, pedophilia) and argues that homosexuality involves compulsive impulses. He states that homosexuality "is not a true illness, though it may be thought an illness in the spiritual sense of 'soul sickness', innate to fallen human nature."<ref>{{cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=jlafJCzJWP4C&q=soul+sickness&pg=PT340 |title=Homosexuality and the Politics of Truth – Jeffrey Satinover – Google Books |date= February 1996|access-date=2012-08-04|isbn=9781441212931 |last1=Satinover |first1=Jeffrey |publisher=Baker Books }}</ref> He also argues that "gay activism distorts the truth and harms not only society, but homosexuals themselves". Most of the book discusses [[whether homosexuality is biological]] and genetic and if it can be changed. About one fifth of the book discusses human sexuality from Jewish and Christian perspectives. In the book's introduction, Satinover states that "[i]n the end the debate over homosexual behavior and its implications for public policy can only be decided conclusively on moral grounds, and moral grounds will ultimately mean religious grounds."<ref>{{cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=jlafJCzJWP4C&q=satinover%20homosexuality%20decided%20on%20moral&pg=PT36 |title=Homosexuality and the Politics of Truth – Jeffrey Satinover – Google Boeken |date= February 1996|access-date=2012-08-04|isbn=9781441212931 |last1=Satinover |first1=Jeffrey |publisher=Baker Books }}</ref>

In 1997, Satinover was called by the State of Florida as an expert witness in Amer v. Johnson, which challenged Florida's law prohibiting adoption by gays and lesbians. "Surprisingly, Satinover said in his testimony that 'if two homosexuals wanted to adopt a child, I would have no objection to it if one of them was a man and one of them was a woman' [but]  'the 'needs' of a child includes having [both] a mother and a father'".<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.onenewsnow.com/Perspectives/Default.aspx?id=140120 |title=Perspectives |publisher=Onenewsnow.com |date= |access-date=2014-03-11 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120726065457/http://www.onenewsnow.com/Perspectives/Default.aspx?id=140120 |archive-date=2012-07-26 }}</ref> He said that "The state of Florida wanted me to argue that the reason the ban should be upheld was because homosexuals made bad parents and I refused to do that."<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.catholiceducation.org/articles/homosexuality/ho0090.html |title=Gay Marriage: Who's Minding the Children? |publisher=Catholiceducation.org |date= |access-date=2014-03-11 |archive-date=2014-03-11 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140311193554/http://www.catholiceducation.org/articles/homosexuality/ho0090.html |url-status=dead }}</ref>   After several years of additional court cases relating to the Florida's anti-gay adoption ban, ''[[In re: Gill]]'' resulted in the ban being declared unconstitutional in 2010.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2008/11/26/us/26florida.html?_r=1 |title=Florida Gay Adoption Ban Is Rules Unconstitutional |newspaper=[[The New York Times]] |date=26 November 2008 |access-date=2014-03-11|last1=Almanzar |first1=Yolanne }}</ref>

Satinover has frequently testified regarding his views on [[same sex marriage]]. In a hearing before the Massachusetts Judicial Committee in April 2003, he testified that homosexuality is not immutable and that the social [[Environment and sexual orientation|environment]] plays an important role in [[sexual orientation]].<ref>NARTH: [http://narth.com/docs/senatecommittee.html "Dr. Jeffrey Satinover Testifies Before Massachusetts Senate Committee Studying Gay Marriage," April 28, 2003] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120313052300/http://narth.com/docs/senatecommittee.html |date=March 13, 2012 }}, accessed March 28, 2012</ref> Organizations that oppose the
